# Mandatory Global AI Rollout: A Change Strategy for a Multinational Insurer

## 1. Reframe: The Mandate Is Measuring the Wrong Thing

The stated problem is uneven adoption. The actual problem is that the program's central instrument — **usage metrics feeding performance dashboards** — is manufacturing the pathologies it is being used to diagnose.

Three predictable effects, all now visible:

- **Performative usage** in high-compliance cultures: query volume rises, value does not.
- **Covert use with suppressed reporting**: employees who find the tool genuinely useful hide that fact, because visible productivity gain reads as *volunteering your own redundancy*.
- **Principled refusal** where professional identity, liability, or law makes the mandate feel illegitimate.

The most important datapoint in the whole program is the covert-use cluster. It proves demand is real and the reporting regime is perceived as hostile. That is a **governance failure, not a compliance failure**, and it cannot be fixed with more mandate.

Second reframe: "resistance follows cultural lines" is only half true. A significant share of what looks cultural is **legal and structural**, and misreading it as attitude will produce a serious mistake.

**Governing principle: mandate the capability and the safety, not the keystrokes.**

---

## 2. Decode the Resistance — Five Distinct Populations, Five Different Interventions

| Pattern | What it actually is | Wrong response | Right response |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Open enthusiasm** | Early value discovery, often in ops/service/distribution support | Hold them up as models to shame others | Convert into pattern authors; harvest their use cases into the shared library |
| **Covert use, low reported usage** | Demand + fear of self-incrimination; also *shadow AI risk* | Enforcement and audit | Amnesty, telemetry firewall, and a credible headcount commitment |
| **Professional-pride refusal** (underwriters, actuaries, claims technical specialists, legal) | Identity and personal accountability under professional standards | "You're behind the curve" messaging | Human-holds-the-pen framing; senior professionals as designers, not targets |
| **Data-privacy / works-council refusal** (DE, AT, IT, NL, FR, BE) | Often a *legal* constraint on performance monitoring, not reluctance | Global uniform dashboard | Co-determination negotiation; jurisdiction-specific telemetry regime |
| **Headcount fear** (ops-heavy hubs, shared services, claims processing) | Rational self-interest under ambiguity | Reassuring adjectives | An explicit, dated, published employment commitment |

In several markets — Germany's §87(1)6 BetrVG, Italy's Article 4 Statuto dei Lavoratori, Dutch and French works-council consultation rights — **a globally uniform individual-usage dashboard may simply be unlawful**. Country teams reporting low usage may be complying with local law while appearing to defy global policy. Verify this before a single conversation about "culture."

---

## 3. Fix the Instrument First (Highest-Leverage Move)

Nothing else works until measurement stops being a threat. Split telemetry into three walled channels with different owners and different access rules.

| Channel | Contains | Who sees it | Who never sees it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Program analytics** | Aggregate adoption, by team, minimum cohort size (n≥15), no individual attribution | Enablement team, country leads | Line managers, HR, performance systems |
| **B — Security & compliance** | DLP, prohibited-data events, model-output incidents | Security/Risk only, under defined trigger conditions | Line management, unless an incident is substantiated |
| **C — Personal insight** | The individual's own usage, savings, patterns | Only the individual; sharing is opt-in | Everyone else, by default |

**Remove individual usage from performance dashboards entirely.** Replace it with:
- **Team outcome metrics** (cycle time, quality, capacity) — what the program was actually bought to move.
- **Demonstrated capability** — certification and a role-relevant work portfolio, assessed once, not surveilled continuously.

What remains genuinely mandatory, and enforceable: complete role-based training; use *approved* tools for any AI-assisted work; follow disclosure rules on AI-assisted outputs; never place customer, claims, medical, or underwriting data in unapproved tools. That is a defensible mandate. "Use it eleven times a week" is not.

A useful internal argument for the change: under the EU AI Act, AI systems used to **evaluate worker performance** fall in the high-risk category (Annex III, employment). Building AI-usage scoring into performance evaluation walks the company toward classification it does not need — while the underwriting and pricing use cases already demand serious high-risk governance attention.

---

## 4. Answer the Headcount Question in Writing

Ambiguity here is the single largest adoption tax. Employees will assume the worst and behave accordingly — which is precisely what the covert-use data shows.

Issue a **Productivity Dividend Commitment**, signed by the Group CEO, with a defined term (24 months):

- No role is eliminated as a *direct consequence* of AI-enabled productivity gains during the term.
- Gains are taken as: backlog reduction, cycle-time improvement, growth capacity, service-quality lift, and **natural attrition absorption** — in claims and ops, typical attrition of 8–12% annually provides real headroom without a single involuntary exit.
- Anyone whose role materially changes gets a funded reskilling path and priority internal placement, with a named guarantee period.
- Publish, quarterly, where the capacity actually went.

If leadership cannot honestly make this commitment, **say so precisely** — which functions, which horizon, what support. A specific, bounded piece of bad news generates less covert behaviour than open-ended silence. Employees are not primarily afraid of job loss; they are afraid of being deceived about it.

---

## 5. Design for Roles, Not for the Tool

Generic "AI productivity" enablement fails in insurance because the work is not generic. Build a **use-case catalogue per role**, each with approved patterns, prohibited patterns, and required human checkpoints.

| Function | High-value approved patterns | Hard boundaries |
|---|---|---|
| **Claims handling** | Document summarisation, correspondence drafting, coverage-clause retrieval, next-best-action prompts | No automated declines; no AI-generated reasoning in the decision record without adjuster attestation |
| **Underwriting** | Submission triage, exposure summarisation, precedent retrieval, referral drafting | No AI-set pricing or risk classification outside governed, validated models |
| **Actuarial** | Code assistance, documentation, literature and regulation synthesis | No unvalidated model output into reserving or pricing; existing model-risk governance applies unchanged |
| **Distribution / broker support** | RFP responses, proposal drafting, product comparison | Regulated-content review before external release |
| **Customer service** | Call summarisation, response drafting, knowledge search | Vulnerable-customer and complaint paths stay human-first |
| **Corporate functions** | Drafting, analysis, meeting synthesis, reporting | Standard confidentiality rules |

Two adoption effects: people stop asking "what do I do with this?", and the professional-pride objection loses its target — because the boundary explicitly protects professional judgment rather than encroaching on it.

---

## 6. Convert Professional Pride Into Program Authority

Underwriters and actuaries resist because their credibility rests on personal judgment and, often, formal professional standards. Do not argue with that. Recruit it.

- **"AI-assisted, human-accountable"** as the standing frame: the professional holds the pen, signs the file, and owns the decision. The tool never signs anything.
- **Senior practitioners as pattern authors.** The reference prompt library for underwriting is written by respected chief underwriters, not by the enablement team. Attribution attached. This converts the highest-status skeptics into the source of the standard.
- **Craft framing over speed framing.** For technical professionals, lead with "fewer hours on retrieval and boilerplate, more on judgment and complex risk," not with throughput. Speed framing directly implies commoditisation of expertise.
- **Publish the failure modes.** Show hallucination examples on real clause interpretation. Nothing builds credibility with expert populations faster than the vendor's own list of what the tool gets wrong.

---

## 7. Shadow-AI Amnesty and Containment

Covert use of *approved* tools with under-reporting is a trust problem. Covert use of *unapproved* consumer tools with claims or medical data is a regulatory incident waiting to happen.

- **90-day amnesty window.** Disclose unapproved-tool use, no disciplinary consequence, help migrating the use case. Contributors to the pattern library get recognition.
- **Make the approved tool win on merit.** Most shadow use exists because the sanctioned tool is slower, more restricted, or lacks the model people want. Fix capability gaps as a P1 backlog, and publish the roadmap.
- **After amnesty, enforce on data handling only** — not on volume. Egress monitoring and DLP as a security control, owned by Security, with proportionate consequences reserved for genuine data exposure.

Declining shadow-tool egress is a *better* adoption metric than rising query counts, and it cannot be gamed by performative use.

---

## 8. Local Operating Model: Global Spine, Local Consent

**Global spine (non-negotiable, identical everywhere):** the safety and data rules; the approved toolchain; the role-based use-case catalogue and boundaries; disclosure standards for AI-assisted work; the employment commitment; the telemetry firewall design.

**Local layer (designed with, not for, each country):** telemetry scope permitted under local law and agreements; works-council/CSE/union negotiation and timing; language and interface localisation; training format and cadence; spokesperson; what "mandatory" concretely means locally.

Sequence matters: **negotiate co-determination markets before the global launch communication reaches them**, not after. A works council that first learns of a monitoring dashboard from a global all-hands will spend the next nine months blocking it — and will be right to.

Deliver through **country leaders and respected local practitioners**, never a headquarters executive on video. In several of these markets the messenger's standing is part of the argument.

---

## 9. Regional Patterns — Read the Driver, Not the Behaviour

| Market | Observed pattern | Actual driver | Intervention |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Germany / Austria** | Low reported usage, formal objections | Co-determination law; monitoring is the objection, not AI | Works-council agreement on telemetry scope first; technical documentation depth; Tier-C personal-only data |
| **Italy** | Low reported usage | Art. 4 remote-monitoring constraints; union agreement required | Union negotiation; aggregate-only reporting |
| **France** | Selective adoption, institutional pushback | CSE consultation, sovereignty and data-location sensitivity | CSE process, EU-hosted processing evidence, formal method statements |
| **Netherlands / Nordics** | Pragmatic, evidence-seeking, quietly high | Wants proof, dislikes ceremony | Open documentation, honest limitation disclosure, minimal theatre |
| **UK** | Compliance-practical, moderate | Consumer Duty and FCA scrutiny of customer outcomes | Map use cases to regulatory expectations; strong QA sampling story |
| **US** | High enthusiasm, high performative risk | Metric-responsive culture | Remove usage from performance immediately or gaming becomes the norm |
| **Japan / Korea** | Low visible use, high covert use, no open dissent | Consensus norms; refusal is expressed as silence, not objection | Very early notice; team-level (not individual) adoption; senior sponsorship; nemawashi before announcement |
| **India / offshore hubs** | Rapid adoption, acute headcount anxiety | Delivery-centre roles most automatable | Employment commitment matters most here; visible reskilling and role-elevation pathways |
| **Brazil / LatAm** | Warm, relationship-driven, uneven | Manager relationship drives behaviour | Invest in first-line managers as the channel |
| **Gulf** | Leadership-driven enthusiasm | National AI agendas, prestige | Executive-level framing plus local capability-building narrative |

---

## 10. Enablement Mechanics

- **Cohort-based, role-specific, protected time.** Four hours a week for six weeks, calendared and backfilled. Un-resourced training reads as an unfunded mandate and produces exactly the compliance theatre now observed.
- **Champion network**, ~1 per 25 knowledge workers, drawn from actual practitioners, with recognition and time allocation. Champions in skeptical functions matter more than champions in eager ones.
- **Manager enablement first.** First-line managers are the transmission mechanism for both adoption and fear. Train them on the employment commitment and the telemetry firewall before employees hear about either.
- **Quality assurance sampling from day one.** Random file review in claims and underwriting for AI-assisted work quality, run by existing QA functions. This protects against the real business risk — silent quality degradation and claims leakage — and gives skeptics a credible answer.

---

## 11. Revised Scorecard

| Category | Metric | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| **Outcome** | Quote turnaround, FNOL-to-decision cycle time, backlog days, first-contact resolution | Query counts |
| **Quality** | Claims leakage rate, rework rate, complaint and ombudsman volume, QA sample pass rate | — |
| **Capability** | % certified by role; portfolio assessments passed | Login frequency |
| **Safety** | Shadow-tool egress trend, prohibited-data incidents, disclosure-compliance rate | — |
| **Trust** | Gap between measured and self-reported use (the covert-use index); engagement-survey items on monitoring and job security; voluntary attrition in high-anxiety functions | — |
| **Value** | Capacity redeployed and where it went; new capability shipped | Cost-per-seat justification |

Track the **covert-use index** explicitly — it is the truest single indicator of whether the trust repair is working.

---

## 12. Sequence

**Days 0–30:** Suspend usage-based performance reporting group-wide. Announce the employment commitment. Publish the telemetry firewall. Open amnesty. Audit which countries' current dashboards are legally non-compliant.

**Days 30–90:** Works-council and union negotiations in co-determination markets. Build role-based use-case catalogues with senior practitioners. Manager enablement. Stand up QA sampling.

**Days 90–180:** Cohort enablement waves by function. Champion network live. Pattern library published with author attribution. First quarterly capacity-dividend disclosure.

**Days 180–365:** Shift the conversation from adoption to outcomes. Expand into governed high-risk use cases (underwriting, pricing) under model-risk and AI Act controls. Report honestly, including where it did not work.

---

## 13. The Strategic Bet

Mandating usage produced measurable compliance and unmeasurable value; it also taught a large part of the workforce that honesty about their own productivity is dangerous. That lesson will outlast this program and contaminate the next one.

The bet is that **removing the coercive instrument increases real adoption** — because the covert users were never resisting the tool, only the surveillance and the implied threat attached to it. Convert the mandate from an obligation to *use* into an obligation to *be capable and safe*, pay for honesty with a written employment commitment, hand design authority to the profession's most credible skeptics, and let outcome metrics carry the accountability that usage metrics were never able to carry.

The organisations that win
